job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Rafael Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do claims accounting at an insurance company in Utrecht, on a graduate scheme that started in September. My day is matching payments to claims, chasing mismatches and writing small notes on why a number is off. I cycle in at eight, have lunch with two other grads on the scheme, and I'm home by six. Two nights a week I coach an under-12 football team, which is the best part of my week. I share a flat with my old teammate Joost, and half my pay goes on rent and my loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it'll save us a bit of time and that's it. At work I'd shrug and carry on. With my mates I'd say every few years there's a thing that's going to change everything and mostly it changes the coffee machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fairly relaxed about my own job, because the scheme is a proper contract and the company needs people who understand claims. What bugs me is money. I've got about three weeks of savings and a loan the size of a small car, and the rent goes up every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job well and try the company's new reconciliation tool when it arrives, since I'd rather learn it than be told about it. I'd put 100 a month toward the loan and keep the football coaching, because it's free and it keeps me sane. In the spring I'd ask my manager about the next level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. A bit like a draw in football: not a win, but nobody's going home sad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your claims work are routine right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot of it. About half my day is matching and chasing, which is the kind of thing software does well. But the notes on why a number is off need judgement, and the claims team still phones me with odd questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does that sit with the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a slow grind. At the current pace it would take me about 11 years to clear it. I'd like to cut that by half, and a raise after the scheme would be what does it, so I'd keep my head down and do well on the scheme.

say: I'd shrug and say it will save us a bit of **time**, and that's it.
With mates I'd say every new thing changes the **coffee machine**, mostly.
think: The scheme is a proper contract, so I feel fairly relaxed about my **own job**.
My worry is **money**: three weeks of savings, a big loan and rising rent.
do: Learn the new **reconciliation tool** as soon as it arrives.
Put **100** a month toward the loan and keep coaching football.
Ask my manager about the **next level** in the spring.
feel: **Okay**, like a draw in football: nobody's going home sad.
S0.quote: Every few years there's a thing that's going to change everything and mostly it changes the coffee machine.
fieldNote: His **contract** feels safe, so the unease comes from rent and loan, not AI.
He treats the tools as something to learn, once others have shown they work.
Football coaching is his free source of calm.

steps.text: Learn the new reconciliation tool when it arrives
Put 100 a month toward the student loan
Ask my manager about the next level in spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and we shouldn't pretend otherwise, but there's also a lot of noise. At work I'd say the company should tell us what it's testing. With friends I'd say it's going to be a decade of the job changing under your feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job's the sort that gets thinner. Matching and checking are exactly what the card talks about. The company would probably keep the grads who can handle the odd cases, but I can see no one replacing the clerks who retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to help test the new tools and write up where they fail, because that makes me useful to the company. I'd start learning data analysis, maybe a short online course on spreadsheets and databases, on Sunday mornings. I'd also hold off on moving to a bigger flat, since rent is my biggest fixed cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit jumpy. Like the first ten minutes of a match when you don't know yet how fast the other side is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your scheme friends. Are they in the same spot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two of the three are in the same spot. We compare notes at lunch. The one in underwriting thinks her desk is safer because her work involves talking to brokers. I'm not so sure, and I don't say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know if your team was shrinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The signs would be small: a retiring colleague not replaced, targets going up, a meeting about efficiency. If three of those happened in a year, I'd start applying elsewhere. I wouldn't wait for an announcement.

With friends I'd say it will be a decade of the job **changing** under your feet.

fieldNote: He has a clear **trigger** list: retirements not replaced, higher targets, efficiency meetings.
Volunteering to test the tools turns a threat into a way to be useful.
He keeps his doubts about a friend's safe desk to himself.

steps.text: Offer to test the new tools and report where they fail

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say honestly that I don't think we'll cope well. At work I'd say the company needs a plan for people, not only for systems. With friends I'd say we should be learning what's happening and not just sharing memes about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job is probably gone by 2028 or at least completely different. Claims accounting is thinking work and rules, which is just what the new thing does. I'd also guess the company would cut grads first because we're the cheapest to let go and the easiest to explain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything but rent, food and the loan, and try to get three months of cash. I'd look for work around real things: a hospital finance office, a football club's admin, a local authority. I'd tell Joost we might need to move somewhere cheaper, and ask my dad if I could stay for a couple of months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and trying not to show it. It's like being told in the 80th minute that the rules of the game have changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. Does the loan change what you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do, because I'd be paying interest on it with no job. I wouldn't be able to ask for a pause until I'd missed a payment. I'd talk to the loan company early and ask about hardship terms, not wait for a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you talk to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joost first, then my dad. I'd also talk to my team's manager, Annelies, to see what she knows. She's honest, and I think she'd tell me. It would be better to know a month early than to be surprised.

say: I'd say the company needs a **plan** for people, not only for systems.
I'd say we should learn what's happening, not share **memes** about it.
think: My job is probably **gone** or completely different by 2028, because claims accounting is rules and thinking.
Grads are the **cheapest** to let go and easiest to explain.
do: Spend only on **rent**, food and the loan, and try to hold three months of cash.
Look at hospital, football club or **local authority** finance jobs.
Ask my dad if I could **stay** for a couple of months.
feel: **Scared** and trying not to show it, like the rules changing in the 80th minute.
S2.quote: Claims accounting is thinking work and rules, which is just what the new thing does.
fieldNote: He sees himself as a **cheap** target as a grad and says so plainly.
He would speak to the loan company early about hardship terms.
Joost, his dad and his manager are the three people he'd trust.

steps.text: Hold spending to rent, food and the loan only

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it gives us enough time if we start now, and I'd say that at work too. I'd ask the company what it plans to do for people in my kind of role. I'd also say that learning something practical, like data, is a good bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd see it as a window where I can reshape myself. By 2031 I'd be 27 and could have a few qualifications and a better cushion. The risk is that five years feels like forever and I spend the first two doing nothing in particular.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish a part-time data analysis certificate in the first two years and look to move into a role that combines claims and analytics. I'd save 150 a month and aim for six months' cash. I'd also try to stay on at the insurer if they will retrain me, because I know the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. Like having the better half of the pitch with the wind behind you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with five years that you can't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years was about surviving. Five is about steering. I'd be able to pick a direction rather than grab whatever's open. And I'd be able to pay down a good chunk of the loan before anything bites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell the under-12s you coach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're eleven. They'd laugh at me if I asked them. I'd tell them to be good at something that needs other people, because that's what a team is. I'm not sure the kids are the ones I'm trying to convince.

I'd ask the company what it plans for **people** in my kind of role.
think: Five years is a **window** to reshape myself and reach 27 with a better cushion.
The risk is spending the first two years doing **nothing** in particular.

S3.quote: Two years was about surviving. Five is about steering.
fieldNote: He sees five years as a chance to **steer**, with a clear certificate plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good time to get ready. At work I'd say we'll cope if the company does it sensibly. To friends I'd say don't panic but don't sit around either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm calm. By 2036 I'd be 32, probably with the loan gone, a flat of my own and maybe a family. The thing I'm careful about is getting comfortable. Ten years of steady work could end with me being the oldest person on the team who never learned the new thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my accounting qualification and move into a team lead role in four or five years. I'd save for a deposit on a flat and clear the loan in about eight years. I'd coach football through it all, and I'd keep trying a new tool every year to stay current.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It sounds like a long, steady season rather than a cup final.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Would you stay with the insurer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, for a while, if it kept being a decent employer. But I'd be open to leaving if something better came up. I don't feel loyal to a company. I feel loyal to my team, and to the kids I coach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you most careful about with a long timeline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being comfortable. I'd put a note in my diary every spring to ask: what would I do if my job was gone in two years? If I couldn't answer, I'd go and learn something. It's the cheapest insurance I can think of.

say: I'd say ten years is a good time to **get ready**, so don't panic and don't sit around.
I'd say we'll cope if the company handles it **sensibly**.
think: By 2036 I'd be 32, probably with the loan gone and a **flat** of my own.
My risk is getting **comfortable** and never learning the new thing.

Save a **deposit** and clear the loan in about eight years.

feel: **Calm**, like a long steady season, not a cup final.
S4.quote: I'd put a note in my diary every spring to ask: what would I do if my job was gone in two years?
fieldNote: Ten years makes him genuinely **calm**, with a deposit-and-family picture.
He builds a yearly self-check to avoid comfort, a very practical habit.
Loyalty is to his team and the kids he coaches, not to the company.

steps.text: Finish the accounting qualification and aim for team lead

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Ten years I can plan around, but two years would catch me with a loan, three weeks of savings and a flat I can't afford alone. What would help is a company that tells us early, some paid time to retrain, and a way to pause the loan if work disappears.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people my age get told it's up to us to adapt. I'm happy to adapt, as long as the people with more room to move than me do some of the adapting too.

headlineQuote: I'm happy to adapt, as long as the people with more room to move than me do some of the adapting too.
portrait: Rafael is a **22-year-old** claims accountant on an insurer's graduate scheme in Utrecht, with a big loan and three weeks of savings.
He's pragmatic and centrist, tries new tools once colleagues have shown they work, and prefers evidence to headlines.
He coaches under-12 football twice a week, which keeps him calm and gives him a sense of purpose.
His mood runs from uneasy to alarmed in the two-year world and settles to calm when he has ten years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because the loan and thin savings would catch him with no time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: Early **warning** from the company, paid retraining time, and a way to pause the loan if work disappears.
